snippet.title: How Women's Maximum-Security Prisons Actually Work | How Crime Works | Insider
snippet.description:
Jacqueline Montanez, formerly known as "Loca D," served 31 years in maximum-security women's prisons in Illinois and Florida.

She was originally sentenced to life in prison as a minor for double murders that she committed at age 15 for the Maniac Latin Disciples, a Chicago gang. Her sentence was later reduced to 63 years after a Supreme Court ruling on life sentences for minors was applied retroactively.

Montanez talks to Business Insider about security, dynamics between prisoners and guards, and gang relationships in women's prisons. She also reveals the details of gang violence, prison economies, pregnancy, and how prisoners navigate romantic relationships.

Since her release in 2022, Montanez has been an advocate for prison reform and has worked with several youth advocacy groups, such as Queens for Queens.

Nick Jones is a former US Marine Raider who served in MARSOC, the Marine Corps’ elite special operations unit.

After starting his career as an infantry mortarman and scout sniper, Jones went on to complete the rigorous Marine Raider training and deployed multiple times to Iraq and Jordan. In 2020, Jones was awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during a chaotic firefight with ISIS fighters in northern Iraq in which he repeatedly charged into enemy fire to rescue wounded teammates despite being shot in the leg himself.

Jones speaks with Business Insider about Marine Raider selection, advanced infantry tactics, and operating alongside allied forces. He goes into detail about the intense realities of close-quarters combat and the firefight that led to his Navy Cross. Jones also reveals the mental and physical toll of combat, detailing his personal struggles with trauma, injury recovery, and alcoholism.

Following his retirement from active service, Jones has dedicated his career to supporting the veteran community. He is the founder of the Talons Reach Foundation, a nonprofit based in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

6 - Disable Social Media Please
Lucrecia Kormassa Koiyan’s story is another example of why social media might be one of the worst things to happen since doctors were telling people that smoking was healthy. The 19-year-old Georgia woman was arrested after disturbing videos surfaced showing her dancing provocatively over disabled men in what appeared to be a care setting.

5 - Glove Dispute 
Some scammers spend years crafting intricate frauds, stealing from family, or targeting the vulnerable. And then there’s Charles Leggett, a man so unbelievably dumb that he turned a minor argument into a crime that instantly put him behind bars—mainly because he essentially confessed on the spot.

4 - The Conniving Jabbing Doctor 
Dr. Thomas Kwan, a 53-year-old general practitioner, disguised himself as a nurse and injected his mother’s partner with a toxin—all in a desperate bid to control an inheritance.  But as investigators unraveled his scheme, they discovered an obsession with poisons that made it seem like this was only the start.

3 - The Promise Of Buried Treasure
Richard Bradley Jr.- a serial…well, you know what usually comes after that…one of those guys- preyed on his victims’ desires of easy money, using a simple yet effective scheme—promising to dig up some buried gold in the wilderness. It was a scam built on trust, one that turned for the worst for anyone who believed him.

2 - The Romantic Rival 
Deon Ramlagan thought he was meeting up with a friend to talk—he had no idea he was walking into a dangerous trap. Betrayed by someone he trusted, he barely escaped with his life, while the two people plotting against him—Arianna Gajraj, a former honor student, and her jealous, low-life boyfriend, Brandon Pirela—ended up behind bars after their plan failed.

1 - The Alpha Business Guru
In a scam that left families drained and desperate, Utah businessman Jeremiah Evans—better known as "The Bull"—persuaded hundreds of investors, including friends and relatives, to pour their savings into his company, Alpha Influence LLC. Promising financial freedom through an Amazon drop-shipping business, Evans and his associates took in nearly $21 million between 2019 and 2022.
